label: Northwestern EDI · Interaction design concept
title: Squad Up
proposition: Turning a messy group order into a shared, visible sequence of joining, choosing, paying, and getting ready.
context: This was a Northwestern EDI team concept created using McDonald’s ordering as the design context. McDonald’s did not sponsor, approve, or participate in the project, and Squad Up was not an official or shipped McDonald’s product.
role: User research · Journey design · Interaction architecture · Prototyping
status: Concept exploration using McDonald’s ordering context

hero.alt: McDonald’s Squad Up interface showing live participant progress
hero.caption: Our team made each participant’s bag a live status signal, so the group could see who had joined, who was still building, and who was ready without another chat thread.

chapters.title: Make the group visible before checkout
chapters.intro: We treated group ordering as a coordination problem rather than a larger cart. The hero shows the intended payoff: a shared state that lets everyone understand progress without one person manually managing the room.
takeaways: Each person keeps ownership of their choices while the group shares progress.
Coordination begins before payment and continues through pickup.

chapters.title: A social stop becomes administrative work
chapters.intro: Across 4 observations · 8 interviews · 22 survey responses, our team saw that McDonald’s often sits between other events. Existing ordering paths forced one person to consolidate choices and chase payment, or left everyone to coordinate separate orders under time pressure.

evidence.alt: McDonald’s research sample showing four site observations, eight interviews, and twenty-two survey responses
evidence.caption: We grounded the concept in 4 site observations, 8 qualitative interviews, and 22 survey responses rather than beginning with interface features.

evidence.alt: Research quote about McDonald’s fitting into an after-class routine
evidence.caption: A participant’s after-class routine helped us frame McDonald’s as a stop between activities, where time and social momentum matter.

evidence.alt: Comparison of group ordering through one payer versus individual orders and payment chasing
evidence.caption: We identified a tradeoff in current ordering: consolidate the food and chase payments later, or separate payment and lose coordination.

evidence.alt: Teen group-ordering problem landscape and needs
evidence.caption: The synthesis connected easy ordering with social reinforcement, financial clarity, and a concept that fits existing teen behavior.

takeaways: The order is part of a social journey, not an isolated transaction.
Payment clarity and group visibility need to improve together.
The experience has to preserve momentum between activities.

chapters.title: One order, individual agency
chapters.intro: We reframed the opportunity around synchronized participation: let people choose and pay with more independence while giving the group one shared path from invitation to fulfillment.

evidence.alt: Opportunity brief for a synchronized multi-user McDonald’s order
evidence.caption: The opportunity brief turned the research into a testable multi-user order with an explicit coordination benefit, interaction risk, and low-fidelity validation plan.

evidence.alt: Squad Up value propositions for payment, pickup, and customization
evidence.caption: We used accurate customization, payment coordination, and pickup or delivery coordination as the three customer-value checks for the concept.

takeaways: Shared does not have to mean one person controls every choice.
The concept must reduce coordination work without adding fragile setup.

chapters.title: The concept had to work before arrival
chapters.intro: We explored kiosk and mobile journeys as distinct alternatives, then resolved the upstream questions both exposed: where a host starts, how invitations travel, and how guests join without assuming the same device or app setup.

evidence.alt: Storyboard of a teen group building and paying for a McDonald’s kiosk order
evidence.caption: The kiosk journey tested separate personal carts and payment methods converging into one coordinated in-store order.

evidence.alt: Storyboard of teens creating a shared McDonald’s order from their phones
evidence.caption: The app journey moved invitation and cart building into the ride between activities, then rejoined the group at pickup.

evidence.alt: Group-order trigger, delivery mode, and invitation setup map
evidence.caption: The setup map made entry placement, pickup or delivery choice, invite channel, and immediate host recognition part of the experience.

evidence.alt: Decision map for app, browser, and no-phone group-order guests
evidence.caption: We preserved three join paths—signed-in app, install-free web, and assisted guest creation—so participation did not depend on one device assumption.

takeaways: Kiosk and app journeys represented distinct context alternatives.
Invitations need to communicate both the host and the commitment immediately.
A no-phone guest remains part of the group state through assisted creation.

chapters.title: Readiness became the coordination engine
chapters.intro: We converted the social ambiguity of “are we all done?” into explicit shared states, then connected those states to invitation entry points and the host actions needed only when progress stalls.

evidence.alt: Shared group-order state from invite opened to all participants ready
evidence.caption: The system map joined invitation, cart, payment, progress, and confirmation into one shared state rather than a set of disconnected screens.

evidence.alt: Four-stage readiness engine for a shared group order
evidence.caption: The readiness engine defined when a member is invited, building, payment-pending, or ready, plus when the host can nudge, wait, or remove an incomplete participant.

evidence.alt: Multiple group-order invitation touchpoints in the McDonald’s app
evidence.caption: The final interaction translated one invitation model across share sheet, QR or tap, and direct recent-squad entry points.

takeaways: Readiness is a system state, not a decorative progress bar.
The host intervenes only when an incomplete state blocks submission.
Multiple invitation modes support different social and physical contexts.

chapters.title: Ownership stays legible through fulfillment
chapters.intro: The final sequence carries the earlier decisions into four concrete moments: understanding the squad, choosing whom to cover, seeing readiness, and keeping individual ownership visible after submission.

evidence.alt: Squad details showing members, cart values, status, and guest addition
evidence.caption: Squad details expose member identity, cart value, payment status, and assisted guest creation in one host overview.

evidence.alt: Squad Up checkout screen for selecting another member’s order to pay
evidence.caption: Delegated payment turns the informal act of covering a friend into an explicit choice before the group order is submitted.

evidence.alt: Waiting for Squad to ready up interface
evidence.caption: The readiness screen proves the state model in the interface by separating complete, priced, and still-incomplete members before checkout.

evidence.alt: Squad Up order completion and pickup interface
evidence.caption: Separate pickup identifiers carry individual ownership into fulfillment instead of ending the shared model at digital checkout.

takeaways: Membership, cost, and readiness remain inspectable before submission.
Payment flexibility does not erase who owns each order.
Fulfillment preserves the group structure through pickup.

chapters.title: A visible sequence for moving together
chapters.intro: Squad Up resolved the concept into a shared sequence from invitation through pickup. The live-progress hero is the clearest summary: individual work remains visible inside one group order, without requiring one person to narrate every step.
takeaways: The strongest design move was making coordination state visible across people.
The concept connects invitation, ordering, payment, readiness, and fulfillment as one experience.

outcome: Our team developed an end-to-end interaction concept that gives a group shared visibility while preserving individual choice, payment flexibility, and pickup ownership. The outcome shown here is a concept and prototype evidence trail, not a measured product launch.
limitation: Squad Up remained a Northwestern EDI interaction-design concept using McDonald’s ordering context. McDonald’s did not sponsor, approve, or participate in the project; it was not shipped, and these artifacts do not establish technical feasibility, adoption, business impact, or real-world usability.
reflection: The project reinforced a durable interaction-design lesson for me: group experiences become calmer when ownership and readiness are explicit states, not information people have to reconstruct through conversation.
